questions.question: What does the name 'Al-Haqqah' — used as the surah's title and its opening word — most precisely convey about the Day of Judgment?
options: A. The terrifying physical noise that will accompany the end of the world
B. The absolute certainty and inescapable truth of that Day, which cannot be denied or avoided
C. The long duration of the reckoning that awaits every person
D. The physical destruction of the mountains and seas on that Day
questions.explanation: Al-Haqqah derives from the root haqqa, meaning 'to be established as certain.' Ibn Kathir explains that this name emphasizes the Day's absolute inevitability — it is the ultimate reality that will expose every deed and leave no room for denial, distinguishing it from the world's temporary illusions.

questions.question: True or false: Thamud and 'Aad both rejected the coming of the Hour (Al-Qari'ah and Al-Haqqah), and this rejection was the core reason divine punishment was sent to each of them.
questions.explanation: Verse 4 states that Thamud and 'Aad denied Al-Qari'ah. The Foundation layer explains that their denial was not merely intellectual disbelief but a willful rejection that led to moral collapse — the same pattern that invites divine retribution in every age.

questions.question: Ibn Kathir identifies the punishment of Thamud in verse 5 as 'al-taghiyah.' What does this term signify in classical Sunni exegesis?
options: A. A drought that lasted for seven years
B. A sudden earthquake that swallowed their dwellings overnight
C. An overwhelming, transgressing catastrophe — the thunderbolt or mighty blast that exceeded all bounds
D. An army of birds that pelted them with stones
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explains that al-taghiyah means a catastrophe that 'exceeds all limits,' identifying it as the mighty blast or thunderbolt that annihilated Thamud for rejecting the Prophet Salih. Al-Tabari similarly notes that the word shares its root with tughyan — transgression — mirroring Thamud's own crime.

questions.question: True or false: According to the surah, the wind that destroyed the people of 'Aad blew for exactly seven nights and eight days, leaving their bodies scattered like hollow palm trunks.
questions.explanation: Verse 7 explicitly states that the wind was unleashed upon them for seven nights and eight days consecutively. The Foundation layer notes this precise duration emphasizes total, relentless divine punishment, and the image of 'hollow palm trunks' conveys that their powerful bodies were emptied of all life.

questions.question: Verse 9 groups Pharaoh, the people of overturned cities (Sodom), and earlier nations together. What lesson does Wahbah al-Zuhayli draw from this grouping for contemporary readers?
options: A. That only ancient civilizations face divine accountability while modern nations are exempt
B. That political power and cultural sophistication offer no protection when a society normalises oppression and moral corruption
C. That punishment is inevitable only for those who reject a physical miracle
D. That the surah is primarily a historical chronicle rather than a spiritual warning
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli notes that grouping Pharaoh — history's most powerful despot — alongside Sodom and earlier nations demonstrates a universal principle: no level of civilizational achievement shields a community from reckoning when it entrenches oppression and ignores divine guidance. He applies this as a warning to modern states.

questions.question: What does verse 17 reveal about the angels on the Day of Judgment that distinguishes this day from all others?
options: A. All angels will descend to Earth to record the final deeds of mankind
B. Eight angels will carry the Throne of Allah above them, while other angels stand on its margins
C. The angels will be given authority to judge each person according to their deeds
D. A single angel will blow the Trumpet while the rest of the angels remain in the heavens
questions.explanation: Verse 17 states that on that Day, eight angels will carry the Throne of your Lord above them. The Foundation layer explains that this is unique to the Day of Judgment — currently four angels bear the Throne, but their number will increase to eight, underscoring the Day's unparalleled cosmic magnitude.

questions.question: True or false: According to classical Sunni scholars, receiving the book of deeds in the right hand on the Day of Judgment is a sign that the person has been condemned to punishment.
questions.explanation: False. Ibn Kathir explains that receiving the book in the right hand is a sign of salvation and success. Verse 19 presents the righteous person joyfully calling others to read his record — 'Ha'umu iqra'u kitabiyyah!' — because it confirms entry into Paradise and that Allah is pleased with him.

questions.question: What is the first cry of the person who receives their book of deeds in the left hand, as described in verse 25?
options: A. 'I wish I had prayed more in my life'
B. 'Would that I had never been given my record'
C. 'I accept my punishment and submit to my Lord'
D. 'Grant me one more chance to return to the world'
questions.explanation: Verse 25 records the condemned person's lament: 'Ya laytani lam utu kitabiyyah' — 'Would that I had never been given my record!' The Foundation layer notes this cry of despair contrasts sharply with the right-hand recipient's joy, illustrating how each soul's record becomes an immediate, undeniable witness against itself.

questions.question: True or false: According to al-Tabari's commentary, when the condemned person says 'my wealth has not availed me' (verse 28), this refers only to material riches and not to social standing or influence.
questions.explanation: False. Al-Tabari explains that 'maaliyah' encompasses all worldly resources — wealth, status, authority, and tribal connections — none of which provide any benefit on the Day of Judgment. The verse strips away every form of worldly prestige that the person relied upon instead of faith.

questions.question: Verse 33 states that the condemned did not believe in Allah al-Azim and did not encourage feeding the poor. How does Sayyid Qutb interpret the connection between these two failures?
options: A. They are unrelated sins that happen to appear in the same verse
B. Neglecting the poor is listed merely as a minor social habit with no theological weight
C. The two failures are inseparable: true belief in Allah al-Azim necessarily generates social responsibility, so abandoning the poor is evidence of hollow faith
D. The verse focuses on personal piety and feeding the poor is only a recommended extra act
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran argues that pairing theological denial with social neglect is deliberate: authentic iman in Allah al-Azim transforms the believer's relationship with society. A person who truly internalises Allah's greatness cannot remain indifferent to the hungry — so indifference toward the poor exposes the shallowness of their claimed belief.

questions.question: What specific evidence do classical commentators cite to disprove the claim that the Quran is the speech of a poet, as addressed in verse 41?
options: A. The Prophet never composed any poetry whatsoever, and the Quran's style differs fundamentally from all known Arabic poetic meters
B. Poetry was forbidden in pre-Islamic Arabia, so the accusation had no historical basis
C. The Prophet was literate but refused to write poetry out of humility
D. Arabic poetry at the time was considered inferior, making the comparison an insult the Arabs would have rejected
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir notes that the Prophet neither composed poetry nor felt inclined to it, and that the Quran's linguistic structure — its rhythms, its legal depth, its narrative sweep — bears no resemblance to the qasida, rajaz, or any recognised Arabic poetic form. Al-Qurtubi adds that this distinction was obvious to the Arabs themselves, who recognised something entirely unprecedented.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 43 affirms that the Quran is a tanzil (revelation sent down) from the Lord of all worlds, directly countering claims that it originates from the Prophet's own intellect.
questions.explanation: Verse 43 states: 'Tanzilun min Rabb al-'alamin' — a sending-down from the Lord of all the worlds. The Foundation layer explains this affirmation closes the surah's refutation of both the poet and soothsayer accusations, grounding the Quran's authority solely in divine revelation rather than any human source.

questions.question: Verses 44-46 state that had the Prophet fabricated anything about Allah, He would have cut off his aorta. What does Ibn Uthaymeen emphasise about this passage as a proof of the Quran's authenticity?
options: A. That it proves the Prophet feared punishment and therefore did not invent the Quran

B. That the hypothetical severity of the consequence — even for the most beloved Prophet — demonstrates no human invention could survive divine scrutiny, and that the Quran therefore must be pure revelation
C. That it warns ordinary Muslims against misquoting the Quran
D. That it establishes the Prophet's personal infallibility in all worldly matters
questions.explanation: Ibn Uthaymeen points out that invoking this hypothetical punishment for the Prophet — the most honoured of creation — proves the absolute seriousness of divine revelation. If even the Prophet would face immediate destruction for fabrication, no human invention could have survived intact. This is one of the Quran's own internal proofs of its divine origin.

questions.question: True or false: Classical scholars understood 'udhunun wa'iyah' (a retaining ear) in verse 12 as referring to those who truly absorb the lessons of Noah's flood narrative and carry them forward — not merely those who hear words.
questions.explanation: Al-Qurtubi explains that wa'iyah means an ear that retains and acts upon what it hears, not one that merely receives sound. The verse calls on those with spiritually attentive hearts to take the story of Noah — preserved as a reminder — and let it reshape their conduct, making hearing inseparable from internalisation.

questions.question: The surah closes in verse 51 by describing the Quran as 'haqq al-yaqeen' — the truth of certainty. How does Wahbah al-Zuhayli distinguish this phrase from the two lower grades of certainty mentioned elsewhere in the Quran?
options: A. Haqq al-yaqeen means the same as 'ilm al-yaqeen and 'ayn al-yaqeen; they are interchangeable synonyms

B. Haqq al-yaqeen is the highest grade: beyond theoretical knowledge ('ilm al-yaqeen) and direct witnessing ('ayn al-yaqeen), it is the certainty that penetrates one's entire being and cannot be separated from the one who holds it
C. The phrase refers only to legal rulings in the Quran, not to its eschatological content
D. Haqq al-yaqeen is a rhetorical device with no precise theological distinction from other certainty terms
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli explains that Islamic epistemology recognises three ascending grades: 'ilm al-yaqeen (certainty through information), 'ayn al-yaqeen (certainty through direct sight), and haqq al-yaqeen (certainty through lived reality). Calling the Quran haqq al-yaqeen places it at the summit — a truth so complete it becomes inseparable from the soul that embraces it.
